title: Scanning Many Genomes for Trait Signals
endLine: Genome scans flag regions linked to a trait, not proven causes.

scenes.tts: How can you find which chromosome spots track a trait like height? Adult height forms a smooth bell curve, even though inheritance obeys Mendel's rules. Many chromosome positions shape height alongside the environment, making it a polygenic trait. Each position is a locus, and its alternative versions are alleles.

scenes.visual: Establish the film's single carried world filling most of the frame height. Upper zone: a crowd of high-contrast person silhouettes rises gently into a smooth schematic bell curve of adult height, with subtle ambient drift. Lower zone: a clean horizontal schematic chromosome track stretches across the frame with pulsing question marks along it as the opening question is spoken. As 'locus' and 'alleles' are named, one person's pair of schematic chromosome strips zooms out smoothly, highlighting one marked spot (label 'Locus') with two colour-coded pill versions (label 'Alleles'). No molecular structures.

scenes.visual: The carried population bell curve and horizontal chromosome track dim slightly in place while continuing slow ambient drift. Clean high-contrast title text 'Scanning Many Genomes for Trait Signals' appears across the centre, holds briefly, then fades away without changing the layout.

scenes.tts: A genome-wide association study, or G W A S, scans many genomes for trait-linked alleles. It counts alleles, not people, since every person carries two copies at each locus. A chi-square score compares allele counts in people with and without a disease to counts expected with no link. The bigger the score, the more surprising the link with the trait.
scenes.caption: A genome-wide association study, or GWAS, scans many genomes for trait-linked alleles. It counts alleles, not people, since every person carries two copies at each locus. A chi-square score compares allele counts in people with and without a disease to counts expected with no link. The bigger the score, the more surprising the link with the trait.
scenes.visual: In the same carried world, a vertical focus band illuminates one locus on the lower chromosome track while several people in the upper bell curve open their two chromosome strips. Two colour-coded allele tokens slide out of each person into a schematic allele-count bar, demonstrating two copies per person rather than one count per person. As 'chi-square score' is spoken, the tokens sort into two schematic allele-count bars, 'With disease' and 'Without disease'; a dashed 'Expected, no link' line sits across both, and a schematic vertical meter beside the locus rises as the 'With disease' bar pulls away from that dashed line (label 'Chi-square score', tagged schematic).
scenes.narration: A genome-wide association study, or GWAS, scans many genomes for trait-linked alleles. It counts alleles, not people, since every person carries two copies at each locus. A chi-square score compares allele counts in people with and without a disease to counts expected with no link. The bigger the score, the more surprising the link with the trait.

scenes.tts: The scan repeats those allele counts across hundreds of thousands of loci at once. With so many tests, some scores run high by chance, so only signals crossing a strict threshold count. Because nearby variants travel together, each measured variant acts as a tag for its region. So genome-wide signals flag associated chromosome regions, not proven causal variants or genes.

scenes.visual: The single-locus beam widens into a smooth glowing scanner sweeping left to right across the entire lower schematic chromosome track. Behind the sweep, a dense schematic landscape of dots rises across hundreds of thousands of loci; a crisp horizontal threshold line (label 'Threshold') cuts across the plot so only a few tall peaks stand out above low background dots. Zooming onto one tall peak, neighbouring tick marks on the chromosome bar bracket together as one shaded block around the measured dot (label 'Tag' and 'Linked region'), illustrating that the signal flags a region rather than one causal gene.

scenes.tts: Test that idea on a new scan. Suppose one tag variant rises far above the threshold in people with a disease. Does that strong peak prove the tag variant causes the disease, or is something missing? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: In the upper zone, the schematic population rearranges smoothly from the height curve into two side-by-side groups (with and without a disease, schematic). On the lower chromosome track, one sharp schematic peak shoots well above the threshold line and glows brightly. A clean question banner appears above the peak: 'Does this peak prove causation?'

scenes.visual: Hold the carried world during the thinking pause with slow ambient motion: the glowing schematic peak stays above the threshold, a gentle pulse ring expands around the tag dot and its neighbouring chromosome loci, and the question 'Does this peak prove causation?' remains clearly visible at top centre.

scenes.tts: No: the peak flags a linked region in one study population, not a proven cause. A shared environment can also mislead, when carriers of an allele also share a diet or upbringing. And population patterns never assign one person's cause. To test mechanism, experimenters edit a candidate gene in animals and compare them with unedited controls.

scenes.visual: The glowing ring over the tag widens into a bracket spanning several neighbouring loci along the chromosome strip (label 'Linked region', schematic), while an ambient tint washes over part of the upper population to represent shared environment (label 'Environment'). A single person silhouette steps forward with a gentle question mark to show a population pattern cannot assign one individual's cause. Then the bracket feeds into a clean side-by-side comparison bar below: 'Edited' versus 'Unedited control' (schematic) testing whether changing one candidate gene alters the trait.

scenes.tts: Adding up small effects across many variants builds a polygenic score. Yet every score inherits the limits of its study cohort. Fahed and colleagues studied U K Biobank, a cohort healthier than the general population. Their scores were less precise outside the mostly European ancestry groups they were built on.

scenes.visual: Across the lower schematic chromosome track, dozens of small peaks send thin light streams upward to combine into one smooth schematic gauge (label 'Polygenic score'). In the upper zone, the population crowd splits into a brightly highlighted study cohort ('UK Biobank', schematic) and a broader, more diverse general population beside it; the polygenic score gauge sits crisp and narrow over the matched group, then widens into a blurred band over groups outside the mostly European ancestry cohort to show lower precision.

scenes.tts: Used carefully, genome scans unlock powerful leads. A 2022 study scanned up to five point four million people for height. It listed twelve thousand one hundred eleven independent variants associated with height. In 2016, Aswin Sekar, Steven McCarroll and colleagues studied the C four A gene. Variants predicted to raise its brain expression were associated with higher schizophrenia risk.
scenes.caption: Used carefully, genome scans unlock powerful leads. A 2022 study scanned up to 5.4 million people for height. It listed 12,111 independent variants associated with height. In 2016, Aswin Sekar, Steven McCarroll and colleagues studied the C4A gene. Variants predicted to raise its brain expression were associated with higher schizophrenia risk.
scenes.visual: The carried population and chromosome track transform smoothly through two human discoveries. First, the upper bell curve of height expands across a vast schematic crowd (label '5.4 million people, 2022') as dense schematic ticks light up across the entire chromosome track (label '12,111 height variants'). Next, the scan zooms smoothly onto one highlighted chromosome region marked 'C4A (2016)', where a schematic expression arrow rises alongside a modest schematic rise in schizophrenia risk.

In 2016, Aswin Sekar, Steven McCarroll and colleagues studied the C4A gene. Variants predicted to raise its brain expression were associated with higher schizophrenia risk.

scenes.tts: Losing C four in mice reduced synapse pruning in the visual thalamus, making that association a testable hypothesis. In 2023, Enbody and colleagues analysed three thousand nine hundred fifty-five Daphne Major finch genomes. Six large-effect loci together explained forty-five percent of beak-size variation in the medium ground finch, leaving most unassigned. Genome scans turn traits into maps that point experiments toward causes.
scenes.caption: Losing C4 in mice reduced synapse pruning in the visual thalamus, making that association a testable hypothesis. In 2023, Enbody and colleagues analysed 3,955 Daphne Major finch genomes. Six large-effect loci together explained 45 percent of beak-size variation in the medium ground finch, leaving most unassigned. Genome scans turn traits into maps that point experiments toward causes.
scenes.visual: The C4 region briefly links to a schematic mouse synapse-pruning indicator that dips when C4 is removed (label 'C4 loss: less pruning (mouse thalamus)', schematic). Then the upper population morphs smoothly into silhouettes of finch beaks varying in size (label '3,955 finch genomes, 2023'), while six bold schematic peaks rise along the lower chromosome track and fill an exact 45% portion of a horizontal beak-size variation bar (label 'Medium ground finch') (computed 45% shaded, the remainder left unshaded and labelled 'Unassigned'). Finally, the chromosome track glows gently as a map with arrows pointing outward toward follow-up experiments.
